btcHoldings.title: Bitcoin holdings and BTC per share
btcHoldings.content:
BTC held is the total bitcoin on the balance sheet at period end. BTC per share (sats) divides that by the assumed fully-diluted share count, in satoshis (1 BTC = 100,000,000 sats) -- the per-share bitcoin backing, independent of the stock price.

For Strategy Inc: holdings reached 847,666 BTC (~99% of total assets) as of Q3 2026, funded almost entirely by issuing convertible notes, common stock and preferred stock (STRF/STRC/STRE/STRK/STRD) rather than operating cash flow -- the software business generates the only operating cash the group has.

What to watch:

  • BTC per share rising even when BTC held is flat (buybacks or a shrinking share base) versus rising only because new shares were issued to buy more bitcoin
  • The pace of accumulation slowing as the share price converges on NAV (see BTC Yield)

btcYield.title: BTC Yield
btcYield.content:
BTC Yield is management's own accretion metric: the percentage growth in bitcoin-per-assumed-diluted-share over a period. It is the closest thing this business has to same-store sales -- it isolates whether issuing shares or converts to buy bitcoin is adding BTC per share faster than it dilutes, independent of the bitcoin price.

For Strategy Inc: BTC Yield was +74.3% for FY2024 and +22.8% for FY2025, but turned negative in 2026 (Q3 2026: -11.9%, 9M 2026: -3.7%) as the share price fell toward its net asset value (mNAV), leaving no accretive room to issue shares or converts to buy more bitcoin per share.

What to watch:

  • A sustained negative BTC Yield means every new share or convert issued is diluting, not accreting, bitcoin per share
  • BTC Yield depends on the market price versus NAV, not on the bitcoin price itself

btcCostBasis.title: Average cost basis vs bitcoin price
btcCostBasis.content:
Average cost basis is the cumulative average price per BTC paid across every purchase to date. BTC price (period end) is the spot price used to mark the holding at that balance-sheet date. The gap between the two, multiplied by BTC held, is the unrealized gain or loss (see the Cost Basis vs Fair Value chart).

For Strategy Inc: average cost basis has risen from ~$30,000/BTC (2022) to ~$75,437/BTC (Q3 2026) as purchases continued through multiple price cycles; the spot price sat below that average for most of 2026, meaning recent purchases are currently underwater even though early purchases are deeply in profit.

What to watch:

  • Spot price crossing below average cost basis -- the point at which the whole position shows an unrealized loss
  • New purchases made well above the existing average, pulling the average basis up faster than the BTC price

btcFairValue.title: BTC cost basis vs fair value
btcFairValue.content:
Cost basis is the total dollars paid for all bitcoin held; fair value is that holding marked to the period-end price. Since adopting fair-value accounting for digital assets (ASU 2023-08) from 1 January 2025, the gap between these two lines flows straight through net income every quarter.

For Strategy Inc: fair value swung from $73.2bn (Q3 2025) to $49.7bn (Q2 2026) to $70.8bn (Q3 2026) on cost basis that only grew steadily -- the chart isolates how much of any quarter's net income swing is bitcoin price, not the software business.

What to watch:

  • Fair value falling below cost basis (the position overall under water)
  • Cost basis growing mainly through new purchases versus staying flat while fair value does all the moving

digitalAssetGain.title: Digital asset gain/loss
digitalAssetGain.content:
From FY2025, fair-value gain/loss marks the entire bitcoin holding to market each period and runs the full change through net income (ASU 2023-08) -- both up and down. Before that, impairment only ever wrote the holding down to the lowest price seen since purchase and never wrote it back up, so pre-2025 net income understated bitcoin's true contribution.

For Strategy Inc: this line, not the software segment, explains why net income went from -$12.5bn (Q1 2026) to +$19.5bn (Q3 2026) in two quarters -- a bitcoin price move, not an operating change. Software segment net income rarely exceeds a few tens of millions a quarter.

What to watch:

  • Read net income alongside the bitcoin price, not in isolation
  • The regime switch at FY2025 means YoY net income comparisons across that line are not meaningful

btcFlow.title: Bitcoin purchased vs sold
btcFlow.content:
BTC purchased and BTC sold are the gross additions and disposals each period -- holdings growth is purchases less sales (plus any accounting reclassification), not purchases alone.

For Strategy Inc: purchases have slowed sharply -- October 2026 added just 778 BTC, the slowest monthly pace in over a year, and Q2/Q3 2026 each included small sales (1,395 and 5,552 BTC) funding preferred-stock buybacks rather than pure accumulation.

What to watch:

  • Sales appearing at all, since the stated strategy is long-term accumulation
  • The purchase pace tracking the gap between share price and NAV (mNAV) -- it should slow as that gap closes

balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Strategy Inc (formerly MicroStrategy Incorporated): equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Strategy Inc (formerly MicroStrategy Incorporated): the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation -- an operating-cash proxy that ignores capital intensity.

For Strategy Inc (formerly MicroStrategy Incorporated): read it beside CapEx: a business that must reinvest most of its EBITDA is not as cash-generative as the margin suggests.

What to watch:

  • EBITDA margin trend
  • Gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow (working capital)

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Strategy Inc (formerly MicroStrategy Incorporated): the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation and interest income -- but for Strategy Inc it is recorded for contract-format reasons only and is not the valuation input.

For Strategy Inc: this business has no meaningful operating cash flow to discount -- FY2025 owner FCF was -$128.8m against net income swings of tens of billions driven by bitcoin's fair-value mark. The valuation below is a bitcoin-treasury NAV model (BTC held × price, less debt and preferred, × an exit multiple to common), not a discounted-cash-flow model.

What to watch:

  • Net income here is overwhelmingly the bitcoin mark, not the software business -- see Digital Asset Gain/Loss above
  • Whether software-segment cash flow alone can cover the ~$1.5bn/year of fixed preferred and convertible-note charges

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Strategy Inc (formerly MicroStrategy Incorporated): the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Strategy Inc (formerly MicroStrategy Incorporated): CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Strategy Inc (formerly MicroStrategy Incorporated): the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Strategy Inc: this is the legacy enterprise analytics/BI software segment only -- roughly $125m a quarter, flat to slightly declining -- not the bitcoin treasury. Software is now under 1% of total assets and is not what this company's valuation is about; see the Bitcoin Treasury section above for the metrics that actually drive the thesis.

What to watch:

  • Whether the software segment keeps throwing off enough cash to cover its own costs (it is the group's only operating cash flow)
  • Interim rows show seasonality, not bitcoin-price effects

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Strategy Inc (formerly MicroStrategy Incorporated): the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
